Meanwhile, a cache sits between your application and the database, holding copies of frequent results so repeated reads skip slow disk work; each cache hit trims latency and lowers load on the primary server during busy hours at peak times.

However, a cache brings risks, because stale entries can outlive the rows they describe. Teams must pick expiry windows, invalidate keys after writes, and monitor hit ratios closely; without that discipline, users may see outdated balances, prices, or inventory counts. Design treats every cache as a tradeoff between speed and freshness, not a free win.

Along with that, data that just sits idle in a full pool of RAM is first to fall. Nothing stops a slow drop, so a hot list of rows with a high miss ratio is at risk. Hit counts, logs, and sums all show a robust story, and that story points a plan.

Finally, measure first, cache only proven hotspots; real traffic reveals winners, so start small and expand slowly. Work is done.
